page.text:
In 1923, John von Neumann provided a celebrated set-theoretic realization
of the natural numbers that solved an ontological puzzle in the
foundations of mathematics. Earlier logicists, such as Gottlob Frege and
Bertrand Russell, had defined the number $2$ as the class of all
two-element sets—a collection that is a proper class and prone to
contradiction unless heavily restricted.

Von Neumann proposed that each natural number be realized as a concrete
pure set whose elements are precisely the preceding natural numbers:
$$\begin{aligned}
0 &:= \emptyset \\
1 &:= \{0\} = \{\emptyset\} \\
2 &:= \{0, 1\} = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} \\
3 &:= \{0, 1, 2\} = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\} \\
S(n) &:= n \cup \{n\}
\end{aligned}$$
In this ingenious encoding, every numeral $n$ has cardinality $|n| = n$,
and the membership relation $\in$ perfectly coincides with the strict
order $<$:
$$m < n \iff m \in n, \qquad m \le n \iff m \subseteq n$$
